AI From Zero

How a small team in Pune built a privacy guard, and learned how AI products are really made

A book to read, not a course to do. Same ideas, same order, same words as the course app, told as one story.

Contents

  1. Before You BeginWhat this book covers, how it is organised, and the people and company whose project runs through it.
1

The problem worth solving

Anaya notices something odd in the chat, and learns how a product person decides what to build, and what to leave alone.

  1. 1The Number in the ChatA product manager finds identity numbers in a week of customer chats and has to decide whether the finding deserves a year of work. Along the way you learn about personal data, counting before deciding, choosing between problems, and writing a decision down.9 min read✓ read
  2. 2Four Questions Before BuildingAn engineer tests a promising idea against the four ways products fail, using a feature that nobody found as the example. You learn the three stages of making a product, the four product risks, and the difference between selling to people and selling to companies.8 min read✓ read
  3. 3Asking About YesterdayA first conversation with a colleague produces only agreement, and five better ones produce evidence. You learn how to question people about their past, how to read what they were trying to achieve, and how to find the one assumption to test first.10 min read✓ read
  4. 4Who Else Is Standing HereA conditional yes from the compliance head sets one hard requirement for the tool, and the product manager then checks what already exists, sizes the market from the bottom up, and studies the competition, including the competitor that is not a product.9 min read✓ read
  5. 5Choosing What Not to DoA list of nine good ideas is not a strategy. A retired teacher's question leads the product manager to write one. She chooses a narrow first target and a single measure of success, names the product, and ranks the work with scores that she is willing to overrule.8 min read✓ read
  6. 6A Plan Others Can BelieveA strategy is a sentence until other people can act on it. You learn to promise outcomes instead of dates, to write goals as measurable results, to map who can say no, and to imagine the project has already failed.9 min read✓ read
  7. 7Writing It Down So Others Can Build ItAn engineer sketches the guard on a napkin and the product manager turns the sketch into a specification that a stranger could build from. You learn the four parts of the guard, requirements and acceptance criteria, thin first versions, and what a paper test shows that a meeting cannot.9 min read✓ read
2

Meeting the machine

What a language model is, how to talk to it, and how to tell whether it did well.

  1. 8What the Machine IsA product manager who has said "powered by AI" for two years tries to explain what it means and cannot. We build the answer from the ground up: language models, tokens, the context window, attention, how a model is made and used, and the two kinds of AI.8 min read✓ read
  2. 9The First ConversationAn engineer shows the product manager a single request to a language model and the reply that comes back. The receipt attached to the reply turns out to teach as much as the answer. You learn about APIs, JSON, API keys, the usage block, and why a confident answer is not evidence.7 min read✓ read
  3. 10A Mind With No MemoryA language model keeps nothing from one request to the next. What looks like memory in a chatbot is the application sending the whole conversation again each time. This chapter shows how that works, what it costs, and why it makes the privacy problem at the centre of the project bigger.6 min read✓ read
  4. 11Giving InstructionsThe team asks a language model to do the guard's work for the first time, and watches it fail in three different ways. This chapter explains prompts, system prompts, temperature, hallucination and worked examples. It also shows the difference between making a failure rarer and removing its cause.8 min read✓ read
  5. 12Knowing Whether It WorksThe team stops trusting how an answer feels, and writes down the correct answers before looking at the tool's. This chapter covers test sets, answer keys, scoreboards, changing one thing at a time, and the five kinds of job a request can be.8 min read✓ read
  6. 13Sorting and SummarisingOne job has a right answer and one does not. The team measures a sorter and finds a failure that a single score was hiding, then checks a summary for the facts it left out. This chapter introduces classifiers, the cost of each kind of error, and the must-keep list.6 min read✓ read
3

Finding things, and the whole machine

Long documents, search by words and by meaning, and how the parts join into one working system.

  1. 14Too Long to Read at OnceTo see how the chatbot answers questions from Sahaj's own documents, a product manager cuts a policy into pieces with scissors, three times. This chapter explains why documents are split, what chunking is, and why no way of cutting is the correct one.6 min read✓ read
  2. 15Finding by WordsA product manager plays the part of the search box. She learns why the oldest way of finding text fails the customers who most need help, and why it is exactly right for an identity number. This chapter introduces keyword search and its silent failure.5 min read✓ read
  3. 16Finding by MeaningA bazaar where shops of the same trade share a lane gives a product manager the picture she needs for the idea that rescued search, and a number to be suspicious of. This chapter introduces embeddings and similarity scores.7 min read✓ read
  4. 17How Good Is GoodA founder asks the question every AI project eventually meets. The answer turns out to be two numbers, a choice between them that is not an engineer's to make, and a figure Anaya had quoted without checking. This chapter introduces recall and precision.7 min read✓ read
  5. 18The Whole MachineEvery part of the chatbot has now been built and broken by hand, so the whole can be drawn from memory and given a name. This chapter introduces retrieval-augmented generation, the ways it fails silently, and the places a customer's words travel.6 min read✓ read
  6. 19Answers a Program Can UseA paragraph is fine for a person and useless to a program. This chapter shows why asking politely for JSON is not enough, how a schema removes a whole family of errors, why the right shape can still hold the wrong content, and how to design a form that leaves no room to invent.7 min read✓ read
4

Giving it work to do

Tools, thinking models, hostile text, grading at scale, and what it all costs.

  1. 20Giving the Machine HandsA twelve-digit order number looks exactly like an Aadhaar number, and the only way to tell them apart is to look it up. This chapter introduces tool calling, tool descriptions, AI agents and step limits, shows how the cost of a loop climbs, and separates actions that read from actions that do.8 min read✓ read
  2. 21Long Windows, Careful RoomsA vendor says a very large context window makes retrieval unnecessary, and a product manager asks the two questions that end the meeting. This chapter shows why what goes into a request matters more than how much fits, and introduces context engineering, token budgets, caching and compaction.6 min read✓ read
  3. 22Machines That Think FirstA model that works out its answer before giving it gets the hard cases right, and takes eleven seconds to do so. This chapter covers reasoning models, what thinking costs, latency, streaming, and a design in which the expensive judgement never makes a customer wait.6 min read✓ read
  4. 23Searching BetterA customer is quoted last year’s late fee. Four improvements to search are measured against the same answer key, and the least glamorous is the only one that can promise a result. This chapter covers hybrid search, reranking, contextual retrieval, metadata filtering and agentic search.6 min read✓ read
  5. 24When the Page Gives OrdersThe guard exists to read what strangers write, which makes it the most exposed program in the building. The team watches a model obey a stranger, and learns the difference between a defence that lowers the odds and one that removes a power. This chapter introduces prompt injection and the lethal trifecta.7 min read✓ read
  6. 25Grading a Thousand AnswersHand-checking stops working at about fifty answers. This chapter covers three ways to mark an answer, how to test a model that grades other models, and error analysis, the most useful quality work in the field, which needs no machine at all.7 min read✓ read
  7. 26What It Really Costs"It depends on tokens" is not an answer to a finance director. A product manager prices the guard properly, finds three very different totals for the same tool, and sees that the order in which the guard’s parts run is the cheapest design decision available. This chapter introduces the cascade.7 min read✓ read
5

The messy real world

Scans and photographs, what you may send, the rules, a spec for a thing that varies, and designing for the wrong answer.

  1. 27Paper, Photos and ScansUntil now, every sentence the guard read was already text. A random sample of fifty attachments shows how seldom that is true of real traffic, and how a capital O standing in for a zero can walk a number past a rule. This chapter introduces OCR and the document audit.7 min read✓ read
  2. 28What You May SendUp to now we have assumed that the text could be sent to an outside company. Three questions, asked in a fixed order, tell you whether it can. Then a vendor's terms of service turn out to say things nobody had read. This chapter introduces retention and data residency.7 min read✓ read
  3. 29Rules, Risk and ResponsibilityLakshmi explains what twenty years in a bank taught her about paperwork. Then the team writes a one-page document that says what the guard is for, what it gets wrong and what it must never be used to do. After that they try to delete one customer and find where that customer's data lives. The chapter covers risk tiers, India's data protection law, system cards, deletion drills, human oversight and shadow AI.9 min read✓ read
  4. 30The Spec for a Thing That VariesA thirty-day notice that a model is being retired shows what a specification must contain when software does not behave the same way twice. It also shows what a switch for turning the AI off should leave running. The chapter introduces rollback, the kill switch and pinned versions.8 min read✓ read
  5. 31Build, Buy or Teach ItA vendor offers to sell the team what it has spent six months building, and a founder suggests training a model of their own. Both ideas sound sensible, and each has to pass the same test. The chapter introduces the AI value chain, open-weight models, fine-tuning and lock-in.8 min read✓ read
  6. 32Designing for the Wrong AnswerAt ninety percent accuracy, one answer in ten is wrong, and what the screen does about that answer decides whether people trust the tool. Then a pilot, designed so that it can fail, gives a stranger result: the system works and nothing changes. The chapter introduces refusals, pilots and failure thresholds.8 min read✓ read
6

Under the hood

The plumbing, choosing a model, retrieval that survives review, agents, voices and pictures, release gates, and assuming the worst.

  1. 33The Plumbing Under the MagicA two-hour outage in which nothing raised an error convinces a product manager that she must understand, at the level of a plumber's diagram, the ordinary software around the one unpredictable part. The chapter covers data contracts, Python, HTTP and status codes, environment variables, Git and experiment runners.7 min read✓ read
  2. 34Choosing a Model on Your Own CasesA founder wants to switch to whichever model topped last week's chart. The team does what you would do with a car. They take three models for a drive on their own roads, record the decision on a card, and then specify exactly what each model sees. The chapter introduces leaderboards, routing, model selection cards and provenance.8 min read✓ read
  3. 35Retrieval That Survives a ReviewA prototype works because you chose every document and you are its only user. Production takes both comforts away. In a review attended by people who would like it to fail, four questions that fit every retrieval system are put to the chatbot. The chapter introduces ingestion, parsers, access control and abstention.8 min read✓ read
  4. 36Workflows, Agents and the Standard PlugA bank teller can look up a balance but cannot send money on a customer's word. Three questions about a support console are settled by crossing things out: how much to let a model decide, how to stop it, and what a standard plug does and does not promise. The chapter introduces tool contracts, idempotency, fixed workflows, bounded agents and MCP.8 min read✓ read
  5. 37Pages, Pictures and VoicesRead a railway timetable aloud, word by word, and nobody learns when the train leaves. The team takes on photographs and voice notes at last. They find the stage at which meaning first goes wrong, and they build a test that can tell a hearing mistake from a thinking one. The chapter introduces multimodal systems, speech-to-text, voice pipelines and speaker attribution.7 min read✓ read
  6. 38Gates, Traces and RollbacksOne edit to one instruction, made late on a Friday night without a test, shows why a change that doesn't feel like a deployment still needs a gate, and why a team should be able to answer "why did it do that?" in forty seconds. Along the way the chapter explains golden datasets, regressions, release gates, observability, trace records, p95 and canary releases.8 min read✓ read
  7. 39Assuming the WorstA compliance report, a Saturday spent trying to break the product with sweets as the prize, and a table in which every safeguard sits next to the test that proves it. The model will be manipulated, so the system around it has to be the defence. Along the way the chapter explains attack surface, least privilege, red teaming, audit trails, risk registers and residual risk.8 min read✓ read
7

A real product, and a job

Shipping it, pricing it, growing it, counting it, running it with real users, and getting hired to do it.

  1. 40A Product, Not a DemoA dish cooked well for two people is not yet an item on a restaurant menu. Before the festival season, the team lists everything that stands between a working prototype and a service, and writes down for each big decision what would make them reverse it. The chapter explains the production delta, graceful degradation, staging, latency budgets, architecture decision records and exit cost.8 min read✓ read
  2. 41Shipping the Whole ThingIn December Anaya stands before the people who doubted the idea and tells them what she built, what broke, who used it, what it costs and what she doesn't know. The eleven stages she followed are the year she has just lived. The chapter explains SDKs, findings documents, failure classes and evidence packs.8 min read✓ read
  3. 42Who Pays, and How MuchA lender's technical lead asks what the guard would cost him. The answer turns on three different people, four ways of charging, and one row of a table that most price lists never draw. The chapter explains seat, usage, outcome and hybrid pricing, contribution margin, flywheels and gross margin.8 min read✓ read
  4. 43How People Find It and StayA tool that nobody finds protects nobody. Five developers are handed a README and nothing else, a stopwatch records where they give up, and a spelling checker shows where the first moment of value has to happen. The chapter explains AARRR, activation, time-to-value, the Fogg behaviour model, product-led growth, growth loops, network effects, virality and dark patterns.8 min read✓ read
  5. 44Counting What MattersOnce real people use the tool, the question changes from "does it work?" to "what do they do?" A privacy product has to answer it without recording anything it exists to hide. A sample-size sum then shows why a young company can't run the test it wants. The chapter explains event taxonomies, tracking plans, cohorts, A/B tests and the minimum detectable effect.8 min read✓ read
  6. 45The Tools and the HarnessA new engineer asks which tool is for what, and an experienced one answers with a drawing of slots, not a list of brands. The same engineer then builds a weekly report twice, once with fixed steps and once with an agent, and the two are measured on the same twenty weeks. The chapter explains toolchains, claim audits, the harness, project memory, allowlists, verifiers, sub-agents, state machines, feature flags, rollback triggers and incident reviews.13 min read✓ read
  7. 46Real People, Real UseA demonstration works while you are watching it. A product has to work when nobody is, for people who owe you nothing. In the spring Anaya prepares the guard for strangers, recruits them honestly, watches without helping, and ships one change because of what she saw. The chapter explains design partners, informed consent, observation sessions, changelogs and support logs.9 min read✓ read
  8. 47The Work, and the JobA former bank analyst has built something real and doesn't know how to show it. Over a few Sunday evenings Anaya helps her turn a year of work into a picture of the jobs she wants, a page of evidence, and a rehearsed way of answering the questions that decide whether she gets them. The chapter explains role matrices, case studies, product sense, system-design interviews, the STAR method and take-home assignments.10 min read✓ read
